extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: A historical overview of the rise and practices of the penny press in 19th-century America, focusing on the New York Sun, the Public Ledger, the Baltimore Sun, and the New York Herald, and including explicit editorial ethics and newspaper mission statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sun's stated object (first issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The object of this paper is to lay before the public, at a price within the means of every one, all the news of the day, and at the same time offer an advantageous medium for advertisements."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mission statement printed at top of the first column of the New York Sun's front page: emphasizes affordable access to 'all the news' plus serving as an advertising medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Ledger — earliest and most useful information for merchants
rubrics_metrics.description: "While its cheapness places it within the reach of the poorest artisan or laborer, we shall endeavor to furnish to the merchant and manufacturer the earliest and most useful information relating to their respective interests."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening-number pledge of the Public Ledger: explicit editorial aim to serve commercial readers by prioritizing timely, useful business information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Ledger — moral and intellectual improvement of laboring classes
rubrics_metrics.description: "It would devote itself with special energy 'to a moral and intellectual improvement of the laboring classes, the great sinew of all civilized communities.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public Ledger's declared social mission: cheap paper intended to uplift and educate working-class readers as part of its purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate party connection to newsgathering
rubrics_metrics.description: The penny press taught the higher priced papers that party connection should be properly subordinated to the other and higher function of the public journals — the function of gathering and presenting the news as it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical normative claim: newspapers should prioritize impartial newsgathering over party affiliation or partisan purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sell news as news, not for effect on readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York Herald was the first to sell news as news and not for the effect it would have on its readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial principle attributed to Bennett and the Herald: prioritize straightforward news reporting rather than shaping content primarily to manipulate reader reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always deal fairly and frankly with the public.
rubrics_metrics.description: "Always deal fairly and frankly with the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the 'constitutional principles' or editorial ethics of the Public Ledger (attributed to managing editor William V. McKean); general injunction about honesty and openness with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give trustworthy information and counsel; do not mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: "A newspaper to be trusted and respected must give trustworthy information and counsel. It is a serious thing to mislead the people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes responsibility of newspapers to be reliable sources of information and guidance; warns against misleading the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understate rather than overstate
rubrics_metrics.description: "Understate your case rather than overstate it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial caution against exaggeration; favors restraint in presentation of claims or accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a sure voucher for every statement, especially for censure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Have a sure voucher for every statement, especially for censure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand for verification and documented evidence before publishing assertions, particularly accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize gap between accusation and guilt
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a wide gap between accusation of crime and actual guilt."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reminder to avoid conflating accusation with proven guilt; requires careful treatment of criminal allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deal gently with weak and helpless offenders
rubrics_metrics.description: "Deal gently with weak and helpless offenders."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical guidance recommending humane treatment in reporting about vulnerable individuals who have erred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand both sides before making judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: "Before making up judgment take care to understand both sides, and remember there are at least two sides. If you attempt to decide, you are bound to know both."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction to pursue balanced inquiry and to seek multiple perspectives prior to passing judgment or editorializing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim knowledge based only on hearsay
rubrics_metrics.description: "Do not say you know when you have only heard."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibition on presenting unverified hearsay as fact; stresses careful qualification of secondhand reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never proceed on mere hearsay; treat rumor as index to inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Never proceed on mere hearsay. Rumor is only an index to be followed by inquiry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic standard to treat rumors only as leads that require verification, not as publishable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Better to be right than first with the news
rubrics_metrics.description: "Take care to be right. Better be right than quickest with 'the news' which is often false. It is bad to be late, but worse to be wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accuracy over speed; explicit admonition against sacrificing truth for timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go to first hands and original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: "Go to first hands and original sources for information; if you cannot, then get as near as you can."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directive to rely on primary sources and eyewitness accounts whenever possible; seek proximity to original information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter chronicles events and collects facts; editor comments
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the reporter's office to chronicle events, to collect facts; comments on the facts are reserved for the editor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines functional roles: reporters gather factual material; editorial interpretation and opinion are the editor's responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let facts and reasoning tell the story rather than rhetorical flourish
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let the facts and reasoning tell the story rather than rhetorical flourish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic principle favoring clear, evidence-based exposition over decorative or manipulative rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be too positive; acknowledge possible error
rubrics_metrics.description: "Don't be too positive. Remember always it is possible you may err."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages humility and caution in asserting conclusions; avoid overconfidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: All persons have equal rights in courts of conscience and law
rubrics_metrics.description: "All persons have equal rights in the court of conscience, as well as in courts of law."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms equal moral consideration for all individuals in journalistic treatment, paralleling legal equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never add fuel to popular excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: "Never add fuel to the fire of popular excitement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against sensationalism that inflames public passions or provokes mob behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual disregard of law is demoralizing in public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is nothing more demoralizing in public affairs than habitual disregard of law."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for respect for law and legal processes in reporting and editorial stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold authorities in maintaining order; rectify wrongs through law
rubrics_metrics.description: "Uphold the authorities in maintaining public order, rectify wrongs through the law. If the law is defective, better mend it than break it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages support for lawful maintenance of order and advocates legal reform rather than extralegal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usually there is law enough; failure is in enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nearly always there is law enough. It is the failure to enforce it that makes most mischief."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation that problems often stem from lack of enforcement rather than lack of legal framework; suggests reporting focus on enforcement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: No excuse for mob law
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no need, and therefore no excuse, for mob law in American communities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit rejection of vigilantism and mob justice as acceptable responses; normative stance for responsible journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep perspective on proportion of 'bad men' to 'millions of the people'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Numerous as bad men may be, remember they are but few compared with the millions of the people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial reminder to avoid portraying society as dominated by wrongdoing; maintain perspective about scale and representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public welfare outranks party cries
rubrics_metrics.description: "The public welfare has higher claims than any party cry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative principle prioritizing public interest over partisan advocacy in journalistic decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace and purity of style desirable but not over rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: "Grace and purity of style are always desirable, but never allow rhetoric to displace clear, direct, forcible expression."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic guidance: value elegant writing but not at the expense of clarity and forcefulness; avoid sacrificing substance to style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain words for all readers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Plain words are essential for unlearned people, and these are just as plain to the most accomplished."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates for accessible language that serves both less-educated and highly educated readers alike; simplicity as inclusive practice.
